sec.title: Background
sec.p: The aim was to investigate if glymphatic function is impaired in patients with Huntington's disease (HD) and its clinical relevance.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Forty‐nine subjects carrying mutant Huntingtin (mHTT), comprising 35 manifest (mHD) and 14 pre‐manifest (PreHD), and 35 healthy controls (HC) were recruited in this study. The diffusion along perivascular spaces (ALPS) index and the percentage of perivascular space in the basal ganglia (pPVS_BG) were obtained in different groups. The discrimination effects of ALPS index were detected using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, and the correlations of ALPS index with clinical features of HD were further analyzed.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: ALPS index was decreased in mHTT carriers compared to HCs, and it was lower in mHD compared to PreHD patients. ROC analysis showed that the ALPS index could discriminate mHTT from HC (AUC [area under the curve] = 0.903), mHD from PreHD (AUC = 0.886), and PreHD from controls (AUC = 0.755). Lower ALPS index correlated with greater disease burden, severity of the disease, lager pPVS_BG, and lower brain volume and thickness of cortices. Regression analysis showed that ALPS index could predict the performance of motor and cognitive functions. Mediation analysis revealed that ALPS partially mediated the effects of CAG repeat and age on the cognitive decline in HD.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: This study demonstrated that the impairment of the glymphatic system, especially in the paraventricular white matter and BG, was correlated with the clinical manifestations, disease burden, and brain structural changes in mHTT carriers. © 2025 The Author(s). body.p: Huntington's disease (HD) is an autosomal dominant, inherited neurodegenerative disorder caused by an abnormal expansion of cytosine adenine guanine (CAG) trinucleotide repeats in exon 1 of the huntingtin (HTT) gene situated in the chromosome 4p16.3 region. 1 Full penetrance is observed at ≥40 repeats and incomplete penetrance between 36 and 39 repeats. The age at HD onset inversely correlates with the length of CAG expansion. The clinical manifestations mainly include motor symptoms, cognitive impairments, and behavioral abnormalities. Clinical diagnosis typically relies on identifying characteristic motor signs, supported by a positive family history and/or confirmed through deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) analysis. 2 There is no broad consensus on the staging of HD, ranging from simple symptom‐based staging to staging based on a comprehensive assessment of the patient's functional abilities. 3 A recent study proposed the Huntington's Disease Integrated Staging System (HD‐ISS) staging framework, which incorporates clinical symptoms and biomarkers. 4 In this grading system, CAG repeat, caudate volume (CAU), putamen volume (PUT), total motor score (TMS), Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT), total functional capacity (TFC), and Independence Scale (IS) were selected as key makers to monitor the disease progression of preclinical patients with a wide range of clinical presentations. However, the heterogeneity of HD presentations 5 has not been considered, and the diffusion brain imaging changes 6 have not been incorporated into the framework.

The glymphatic pathway was initially identified in rodent brains, and it involves the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flowing into the brain parenchyma through the perivascular space of arteries, subsequently flowing into the interstitial space and perivenous spaces in sequence. 7 The convective influx of the CSF is balanced by the perivenous efflux of the interstitial fluid. 7 In this glymphatic pathway, fluid flows can collect and clear neurotoxic waste metabolites. 8 Recent evidence emphasizes the role of the glymphatic system in eliminating neurotoxic protein aggregations in neurodegenerative diseases, such as amyloid‐β in Alzheimer's disease (AD), 9 , 10 , 11 α‐synuclein in Parkinson's disease (PD), 12 , 13 and trans‐activation response (TAR) DNA‐binding protein 43 (TDP43) in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD). 14 HD is also an abnormal protein deposition–related neurodegenerative disorder, but whether glymphatic system function is impaired in the disease is not well known.

Several methods have been developed to assess glymphatic function, including intrathecal or intravenous use of gadolinium‐based contrast agents (GBCA), perivascular space volume (PVS), choroid plexus volume, and the index for diffusion tensor image analysis along the perivascular space (ALPS). 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 PVS in the basal ganglia (PVS_BG) has been related to the glymphatic system function in cerebral small vessel disease 20 , 21 as well as in AD. 22 The ALPS index, a noninvasive method that can evaluate water diffusivity around the lateral paraventricular white matter, has been widely employed in various neurodegenerative disorders for research on the glymphatic system, such as AD, 23 , 24 PD, 25 , 26 FTD, 14 and ALS, 27 given its high sensitivity of reflecting glymphatic function. 19

In this context, we hypothesized that abnormal protein accumulation in HD might impair glymphatic function, similar to other neurodegenerative diseases, which in return would further affect the clearance of abnormal protein and impact on the clinical symptoms and disease progression of HD. Therefore, in this study, we utilized the ALPS index and the percentage of PVS_BG (pPVS_BG) in a cohort carrying mutant HTT (mHTT) to investigate the function of the glymphatic system and further explore the possible role of the glymphatic pathway in the heterogeneity of HD.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: Between May 2019 and October 2023, 49 mHTT carriers were recruited from the Neurogenetic Outpatient Clinic at Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University, along with 35 age‐ and sex‐matched healthy controls (HC) recruited from the community. After participants who did not meet the imaging quality standards were excluded, mHTT carriers were further classified into pre‐manifest HD (PreHD, 14 subjects) and manifest HD (mHD, 35 subjects) groups based on TMS ≥5. 28

Inclusion criteria for the mHTT gene carrier group were as follows: (1) age ≥18 years; (2) confirmed presence of >35 CAG repeats in exon 1 of HTT using polymerase chain reaction (PCR), Southern blot hybridization, or triple repeat primer PCR 29 ; (3) physically capable of completing the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination; and (4) signed the informed consent. Inclusion criteria for the control group were as follows: (1) age ≥18 years, (2) no genetic or clinical evidence for the presence of neurological disorders, and (3) signed the informed consent. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) history of severe stroke, brain trauma, epilepsy, or mental illness; (2) history of brain tumor and space occupation; (3) history of other central nervous system degenerative diseases; (4) patients unable to complete the magnetic resonance examination; and (5) refusal or inability to provide informed consent.

This study received ethical approval from the Research Ethics Committee of Beijing Tiantan Hospital, Capital Medical University (KY 2018‐031‐02). Participants provided written consent after they had been fully informed.

sec.title: Clinical Assessments
sec.p: Demographic information—such as age, onset age, family history, duration of motor, cognitive, and psychiatric symptoms, and the number of CAG repeats in the HTT gene—was recorded. We computed the CAG‐age product (CAP) score for each mHTT carrier using the standardized formula CAP = age(CAG repeat length – 33.66), 30 indicating that the CAP score reflected the disease burden. Demographic information and Mini‐Mental State Examination (MMSE) 31 score were collected for all control participants in this study, following the same procedures as for mHTT participants. Additionally, we administered the Unified Huntington's Disease Rating Scale assessments for all enrolled subjects, including TMS, TFC, and IS, and cognitive changes were assessed using the SDMT. 32

sec.title: MRI Acquisition
sec.p: MRI scans, including 3D T1 and 3D T2 images and diffusion MRI (dMRI), were performed on a Siemens Prisma 3‐T MRI scanner equipped with a 64‐channel head coil for each participant. Throughout the scanning procedure, participants remained awake with their eyes closed and their heads immobilized, ensuring minimal motion; the scanning parameters are as follows: 3D T1 MPRAGE scanning parameters: voxel size, 0.9 × 0.9 × 1.0 mm; field of view (FoV) read, 240 mm; FoV phase, 100%; repetition time (TR), 1560 ms; Echo Time (TE), 1.69 ms; slice resolution, 100%; flip angle, 8°; sagittal slices, 176; 3D T2 scanning parameters: voxel size, 0.9 × 0.9 × 1.0 mm; FoV read, 230 mm; FoV phase, 100%; TR, 3000 ms; TE, 409 ms; slice resolution, 100%; flip angle, 8°; sagittal slices, 192; dMRI collected with multishell data for other diffusion kurtosis imaging studies 6 , 33 : 129 gradient directions and B values of 0, 1000, and 2000; voxel size, 2.5 × 2.5 mm; FoV read, 220 mm; FoV phase, 100%; TR, 2900 ms; and TE, 64 ms.

sec.title: dMRI Processing and ALPS Calculating Protocol
sec.p: All processing steps were performed using the DSI Studio GUI. 34 The four‐dimensional dMRI volume DICOM files were initially converted to SRC files. Subsequently, the images were preprocessed using TOPUP/EDDY and motion correction programs to address phase distortion, eddy current, and motion issues.

The spatial normalization of the diffusion information was conducted using the Q‐space diffeomorphic reconstruction (QSDR) method, which automatically transformed the images into the MNI (Montreal Neurological Institute) space and normalized them to the ICBM152_adult template. Tensor calculations were performed only at b‐value = 1000, 15 using the “no high b” option. According to the previous DTI‐ALPS studies, region of interest (ROI) is placed on the projection fibers and associated fibers adjacent to the lateral ventricle at the level of the lateral ventricle body to evaluate the movement of water molecules along the X‐axis. 24 Four ROIs were placed on the color‐coded fractional anisotropy (FA) and diffusivity maps of each subject, respectively. To avoid possible deviations in ROI placement and ensure the accuracy of fiber determination, the placement of ROI was confirmed by two experienced personnel (Intraclass Correlation Coefficient, ICC = 0.96). Subsequently, the bilateral diffusivity values of Dxx, Dyy for the projection (Dxxproj, Dyyproj) and the bilateral Dxx, Dzz for the association (Dxxassoc, Dzzassoc) fibers were obtained for the ALPS calculation (Fig. 1). ALPS index was calculated using the formula: ALPS = mean (Dxxproj, Dxxassoc)/mean (Dyyproj, Dzzassoc). 24 The mean values of the left and right ALPS (mALPS) indices and the mean values of Dxxproj (mDxxproj), Dxxassoc (mDxxassoc), Dyyproj (mDyyproj), and Dzzassoc (mDzzassoc) were evaluated. Furthermore, FA and mean diffusivity (MD) values were extracted using the same ROIs. The mean FA and MD (mMD) values of bilateral projection and association fibers were calculated.

sec.title: Structural MRI Preprocessing Protocol
sec.p: Structural images were preprocessed using the CAT 12 within the SPM12 software. DICOM format images were converted to the NIFTI format and subjected to spatial normalization. Subsequently, gray matter, white matter, and CSF images, obtained through segmentation, were standardized to the MNI standard space with a voxel size of 1.5 × 1.5 × 1.5 mm. Normalized structural images in the MNI space were registered to the Automated Anatomical Labeling Atlas 3 map. 35 Subsequently, surface and thickness estimations were performed using CAT12, according to the HD‐ISS system 4 and HD gray matter analysis. 36 Finally, volumes of neostriatum (NE, encompassing bilateral CAU and PUT), pallidum (PAL), insula (INS), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), middle temporal gyri (MTG), left dorsolateral superior frontal gyrus (LSFG), total intracranial volume (TIV), and cortical thickness were obtained. 4 To avoid the interferences of individual TIV differences, the ratio of each brain region volume (CAU, PUT, PAL, INS, ACC, MTG, and LSFG) to TIV was utilized for subsequent statistical analysis.

sec.title: Automatic pPVS_BG Quantification Protocol
sec.p: PVS mapping was performed using a recently developed technique by Sepehrband et al. 37 First, T1w and T2w images were generated in the PVS map using the enhanced PVS contrast (EPC) method. 38 Advanced Normalization Tools 39 software package was used to perform field bias correction to EPC images. Then the FMRIB Software Library (FSL) software 40 was used to perform skull stripping, and linear with nonlinear method was used to transform them into MNI space. The next step was to use Quantitative Imaging Toolkit software 41 to perform Frangi filtering after nonlocal means filtering onto the EPC images. The Frangi filter estimated a vesselness measure for each voxel from eigenvectors of the Hessian matrix of the image. The default setting for Frangi filter implementation was used as recommended in Frangi et al. 42 Vesselness threshold was 1.5 in this study, as suggested in a previous study. 37 Then, an experienced radiologist visually evaluated the automatic segmentation results and adjusted the algorithm for the segmentation results with significant anomalies. If there are still significant errors after adjusting the algorithm, they will be excluded. Finally, we used FSL and FreeSurfer to obtain PVS volume in the BG of each participant, and the percentages of PVS volume in BG (pPVS_BG) were calculated.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: For clinical data, the Shapiro–Wilk test was applied to assess normality. Normally distributed data were presented as mean ± standard deviation, whereas nonnormally distributed data were expressed as median ± interquartile range. The χ2 test was used to compare gender composition differences among groups. Univariate general linear model with bootstrap was employed to compare the variables between groups, with age as covariate. Partial correlation analysis was applied to investigate ALPS index relationship with clinical assessments, disease burden, and structural MRI parameters in mHTT carriers, with age as covariate. Values of P < 0.05 after false discovery rate (FDR) correction were considered statistically significant. Subsequently, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were utilized to assess the diagnostic performance of the ALPS index in discriminating between different groups. Multivariate linear analyses were conducted to explore whether the ALPS index is an independent factor for motor, cognitive, or overall function in HD patients. Finally, structure equation modeling (SEM) analyses were carried out to explore the mediating role of ALPS in the relationship between CAG repeat number, age, clinical performances, and MRI parameters. To process the missing values, the missing variables were removed during data analysis. The aforementioned statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS 26.0, GraphPad Prism 9.0, and IBM SPSS Amos 26 when appropriate.

sec.title: Demographic and Clinical Information Difference between Groups
sec.p: Significant differences were observed in the mean age among the HC, PreHD, and mHD groups; mean age in the PreHD group was significantly younger than that in the HC and mHD groups (Table 1). Cognitive function (MMSE) in the mHD group was significantly impaired compared to that in the HC and PreHD groups (Table 1). CAP scores in the PreHD group were significantly lower than those in the mHD group, whereas TMS was significantly increased in the mHD group compared with the PreHD group (Table 1). Cognitive assessments scores, including SDMT and MMSE, in the PreHD group were higher than those in the mHD group (Table 1). TFC and IS were significantly lower in the mHD group compared with the PreHD group (Table 1).

sec.title: Structural MRI in Different Groups
sec.p: All participants in this study underwent MRI acquisition. After GLM analysis, CAU/TIV, PUT/TIV, PAL/TIV, INS/TIV, MTG/TIV, and cortical thickness showed significant differences between any two groups, with HCs > PreHD > mHD (Table 1). The mean cortical thickness in the mHD group was significantly less than that in either the HC or PreHD group, but no significant difference was observed between the HC and the PreHD groups (Table 1). The other structural ratio, including ACC/TIV and LSFG/TIV, in the HC group was significantly higher than that in any other two groups. The ACC/TIV and LSFG/TIV in the PreHD group was higher than that in the mHD group, but the difference did not reach statistical significance (Table 1).

sec.title: ALPS Index, pPVS_BG, FA, and MD among Three Groups
sec.p: There were significant differences in the mALPS index (P < 0.0001, η2 = 0.582) and pPVS_BG values (P < 0.0001, η2 = 0.366) among the three different groups (Fig. 2). Post hoc analysis revealed that mALPS index was the highest in HCs, followed by PreHD, and the lowest in mHD, and the mALPS in PreHD was significantly lower than that in HCs (Fig. 2A). The pPVS_BG values in mHD were the highest in mHD, followed by PreHD, and the lowest in HCs (Fig. 2B). In contrast with the ALPS index, the η2 value of the three groups was lower, and the P‐value of PreHD compared with the other two groups was higher (Fig. 2B). To avoid the results being affected by age differences between HCs and PreHD, we compared mALPS and pPVS_BG differences between these two groups using propensity scores matching, and the results obtained were similar to earlier results (Table S1).

sec.p: The mDxxproj, mDxxassoc, mDyyproj, and mDzzassoc did not exhibit significant differences among the three groups, although mMD values in the mHD group were significantly higher than those in the HCs (P = 0.04, Table S2).

sec.title: ROC Analysis in Discrimination of Different Groups Using ALPS or pPVS_BG
sec.p: ROC analysis was performed to assess the performance of ALPS or pPVS_BG in differentiating between groups. The ALPS index showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.903 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.839–0.967) to distinguish mHTT carriers from HCs with a cutoff value of 1.566 and a Youden index of 0.698 (Fig. 3A), which was much better than pPVS_BG (Fig. 3D, AUC = 0.836). ROC analysis showed that the ALPS index was effective in discriminating between PreHD and mHD, with an AUC of 0.886 (95% CI 0.780–0.991) when the cutoff value was 1.527 and the Youden index was 0.714 (Fig. 3B), whereas the AUC was 0.769 for pPVS_BG (Fig. 3E). ROC analysis showed that the ALPS index discriminated PreHD from HCs with a fair predication value (AUC = 0.755, 95% CI 0.614–0.896) with a cutoff value of 1.792 and a Youden index of 0.457 (Fig. 3C). In addition, pPVS_BG has a relatively less but acceptable predictive power to discriminate PreHD from HCs (AUC = 0.716, 95% CI 0.552–0.880) (Fig. 3F).

sec.title: Correlation Analysis between ALPS/pPVS_BG Index and Clinical Characteristics
sec.p: After FDR correction, the ALPS index exhibited a negative correlation with CAP scores (r = −0.372, FDR‐P = 0.013) and TMS (r = −0.535, FDR‐P = 0.0004), as well as a positive correlation with TFC (r = 0.409, FDR‐P = 0.008), IS (r = 0.382, FDR‐P = 0.007), and SDMT (r = 0.478, FDR‐P = 0.001) (Fig. S1). Furthermore, partial correlation analysis between ALPS and other image indicators showed a positive correlation between ALPS and CAU/TIV (r = 0.486, FDR‐P = 0.0004), PUT/TIV (r = 0.493, FDR‐P = 0.0004), PAL/TIV (r = 0.474, FDR‐P = 0.003), MTG/TIV (r = 0.425, FDR‐P = 0.007), and mean cortical thickness (r = 0.308, FDR‐P = 0.04), as well as a negative correlation with mMD (r = −376, FDR‐P = 0.01). In addition, the ALPS index had a negative correlation with pPVS_BG (r = −0.391, FDR‐P = 0.0004) (Fig. S1).

The pPVS_BG exhibited a positive correlation with CAP scores (r = 0.365, FDR‐P = 0.035), as well as a negative correlation with CAU/TIV (r = −0.586, FDR‐P = 0.008), PUT/TIV (r = −0.582, FDR‐P < 0.0001), and PAL/TIV (r = −0.514, FDR‐P = 0.002) (Fig. S1).

sec.title: Identifying Predicative Factors for the Clinical Performance of HD
sec.p: Multivariate linear regression analysis, including the variables age, CAG repeats, ALPS index, pPVS_BG, NE/TIV, PAL/TIV, INS/TIV, ACC/TIV, MTG/TIV, LSFG/TIV, and cortical thickness, was conducted to determine the predicative factors for motor and cognitive function in HD. We found that NE/TIV was the most significant predictive factor for clinical performance in the motor function of TMS (β = −0.468, P = 0.001) and the cognitive function of SDMT (β = 0.510, P = 0.0003). mALPS was another independent predicative factor for TMS (β = −0.362, P = 0.007) and SDMT (β = 0.312, P = 0.022) in mHTT carriers (Table S3). We did not find that age, CAG repeat number, pPVS_BG, or any other brain structural changes had significant predictive effects on TMS or SDMT.

sec.title: SEM Analysis for Evaluating ALPS Index Mediation Effects
sec.p: In the SEM analysis to evaluate the ALPS index mediation effects, we chose SDMT, TMS, TFC, and IS as the clinical performance indicators of HD. The results showed that mALPS demonstrated significant mediating effects on the relationship between CAG repeats and age on SDMT (Fig. 4). The total effect of CAG on SDMT was β = −0.374, of which mALPS contributed a mediation effect of β = −0.125. The total age on the SDMT effect was β = −0.699, including the indirect effect of β = −0.230 from mALPS (Fig. 4). mALPS decline accounted for ~ 33.4% of the total CAG repeat effect and 32.9% of the total age effect on SDMT performance, but no mediating effect of mALPS on CAG repeats and age on TMS, TFC, IS, and brain structure.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study applying ALPS index along with PVS analysis for glymphatic function research in HD. We found that the ALPS index, whose ROIs were placed on paraventricular white matter, was a more sensitive tool than pPVS_BG, whose ROIs were placed on the BG, in detecting glymphatic system dysfunction. The ALPS index can serve as an independent factor reflecting the disease progression and clinical presentations of HD.

An analysis of the brain regional volume changes and the average thickness of the cortex (Table 1) showed that the neostriatal and cortical atrophy occurred in the early stage of HD. This result aligns with previous studies 43 , 44 , 45 and is in agreement with the notion of neostriatal NE volume changes as a biomarker for the progression of HD. 4

Glymphatic system impairment in HD identified by ALPS was confirmed using pPVS_BG analysis (Fig. 2). Similar to previous findings, 46 , 47 the pPVS_BG was significantly different between HCs and PreHD. However, the difference in mALPS index between groups was more significant than that in pPVS_BG (Fig. 3; Table S1), suggesting ALPS is a more sensitive tool in detecting glymphatic system dysfunction. The significant difference between HCs and PreHD in ALPS suggested that the damage to the glymphatic system occurs prior to the onset of dominant symptoms in HD due to the presence of the disease‐causing gene, which is consistent with a previous study in AD showing less‐efficient fluid transport along the perivascular pathway and compromised glymphatic clearance indicated by decreased ALPS index measures. 24 Indeed, the perivascular space is a key site of the glymphatic system, 48 and the integrity of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) in HD has been shown to be damaged. 49 Animal studies also showed that mHTT protein could be cleared by the glymphatic system into the CSF and blood and a significant decrease in CSF clearance efficiency in HD mice prior to phenotypic onset. 50 , 51 These results suggested that an impaired glymphatic system function occurred at the early stage of HD. According to previous literature, the projection fibers at the body level of the lateral ventricle are the superior corona radiata, and the associated fibers are the superior longitudinal fasciculus. Our previous studies confirmed that these two fiber bundles are microstructurally altered in HD. 6 But because the ROI does not include the entire fiber, this placement principle has been applied in a variety of diseases. 18 , 34 At present, there is no sufficient evidence for the potential association of ALPS ROI with specific diseases.

When the disease manifested, the glymphatic system function was further impaired, with the ALPS index lower in mHD compared to PreHD (Figs. 2 and 3). The decrease in ALPS in the disease group was also observed in other neurodegenerative diseases such as AD, 52 , 53 PD, 25 FTD, 14 and ALS. 27 Correlation analysis showed that the ALPS negatively correlated with CAP. The result suggested that greater disease burden was associated with greater glymphatic dysfunction. Similarly, ALPS index has been shown to be negatively correlated with the degree of Aβ and tau deposition, which represents the disease burden of AD. 53 ROC analysis revealed a high accuracy of using ALPS index to distinguish mHD from PreHD (Fig. 3). This indicated that the ALPS index had a good distinguishing effect in different periods of mHTT carriers.

Our data (Fig. S1) confirmed that an enlarged PVS correlated with cognitive dysfunction and disease burden in HD patients, 46 , 47 and we also showed that enlarged pPVS_BG was correlated with BG volume and mALPS index. A comparison of the pPVS_BG and ALPS results showed that the ALPS index was more obvious and sensitive to the changes in HD than pPVS_BG. Our partial correlation analysis revealed that the ALPS positively correlated with the relative volume of the NE and the mean cortical thickness, which was consistent with previous reports of a negative association between enlarged PVS and NE volume in HD patients. 46 , 47 Our study further elucidated the positive correlation between glymphatic system dysfunction and the atrophy of CAU, PUT, PAL, and MTG and cortical thickness through ALPS index in mHTT carriers. The correlation of ALPS index with brain atrophy in HD is consistent with previous findings in AD 54 and cerebral small vascular disease. 55

Our results showed that the ALPS index significantly correlated with other key indicators in HD‐ISS, including disease burden, SDMT, and TMS after multivariate linear regression, which were similar to previous findings in AD, PD, and FTD showing that the ALPS index was significantly correlated with cognitive 14 , 18 , 52 , 56 and motor function. 25 , 56 ALPS partially mediated the effect of CAG and age on SDMT in mHTT carriers (Fig. 4). That is, higher CAG repeats and older age associated with more severe impairment of glymphatic system function, which may contribute to more severe cognitive dysfunction in HD patients. Similarly, the mediation effect of ALPS on the relationship between disease duration and cognitive impairment had been found in patients with PD. 26 Our results suggested that the impairment of the glymphatic system might affect the elimination of mHTT protein and other related metabolic wastes, thereby affecting the symptoms of HD patients.

The present study has several limitations. First, this was a single‐center study with a relatively small number of participants, and the results might need to be validated in another cohort. Second, this is a cross‐sectional study. Our results may not fully reflect the changes in the ALPS index in the progression of HD. Finally, GBCA MRI, the current gold standard to assess glymphatic function, 15 was not performed in this study due to its invasive nature. Because ALPS and PVS are indirect measures of glymphatic system function, and the ALPS index can assess water diffusion only in the paraventricular white matter but not the entire brain, 57 , 58 , 59 their detection of glymphatic system function in HD might not be effective, although significant correlation between the ALPS index and the signal unit ratio of GBCA MRI has been reported, 19 suggesting that ALPS partially reflects the glymphatic system function of the entire brain.

In conclusion, we confirmed the impairment of the glymphatic system in mHTT carriers. The ALPS index was a more sensitive approach than pPVS_BG in detecting glymphatic system dysfunction in HD. The glymphatic system impairment identified by the ALPS index was correlated with clinical manifestations, disease burden, and brain structural changes in mHTT carriers. However, the glymphatic system dysfunction in HD may need to be further explored by large‐scale longitudinal studies and comprehensive analysis using different methods. It suggests that enhancing glymphatic function may be a feasible strategy for the treatment of HD, and those approaches demonstrated that glymphatic and/or meningeal lymphatic system amelioration in AD 60 , 61 might be effective in HD.
